section_summary: This section documents diplomatic exchanges and interdepartmental coordination from September 1934 to September 1935 concerning the exemption of non-diplomatic foreign officials from United States Federal income taxation. Initiated when the Treasury Department required departing Japanese railway official Yorio Yamamoto and colleagues in New York to post surety bonds for unpaid taxes, the Japanese Embassy sought reciprocal tax exemptions for unaccredited personnel. The State Department and Treasury coordinated with Congress to resolve the statutory barrier, culminating in the introduction and enactment of H.R. 7998 (approved August 27, 1935), which amended the Revenue Act to authorize reciprocal tax exemptions for foreign government employees upon State Department certification.

subfiles.about: Reports on inquiries made with the Treasury Department regarding the requirement that Japanese railway official Yorio Yamamoto pay income tax before sailing from New York.
subfiles.summary: A representative of the Japanese Embassy, Mr. Tsuchiya, requested that the Treasury Department extend income tax courtesies to Yorio Yamamoto, an official of the Imperial Japanese Railway Department leaving New York for England. The State Department consulted Treasury officials, who cited a recent ruling that foreign officials without diplomatic or consular status are subject to Federal income tax. Revenue officials suggested that Yamamoto confer with the revenue agent in charge in New York to obtain departure clearance, which advice was relayed to Tsuchiya.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Income Tax Status and Departure of Yorio Yamamoto

subfiles.about: Requests that Yorio Yamamoto of the Imperial Japanese Railway Department be granted traditional courtesies and exempted from income tax upon applying for a sailing permit.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Yorio Yamamoto, an official of the Imperial Japanese Railway Department stationed in New York for three years, was requested by the Treasury Department to pay income taxes upon applying for a sailing permit for England. The memorandum requests that the United States Government extend the usual courtesies accorded to such officers and treat Mr. Yamamoto in the same manner as his predecessors.
subfiles.title: Aide-Mémoire regarding Income Tax Exemption for Yorio Yamamoto

subfiles.about: Inquires whether the Office of the Legal Adviser prefers to draft a reply to the Japanese Embassy regarding Yorio Yamamoto.
subfiles.summary: Eugene H. Dooman of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs transmits a handwritten note to William R. Vallance in the Office of the Legal Adviser. Dooman inquires whether Vallance would prefer to draft the Department's response to the Japanese Embassy's note.
subfiles.title: Routing Slip regarding Draft Reply to Japanese Embassy

subfiles.about: Informs the Secretary of State that Yorio Yamamoto departed on bond and requests State Department good offices in adjusting his tax liability.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Chargé d'Affaires ad interim informs Secretary Hull that Yorio Yamamoto, Secretary of the Japanese Department of Railways studying railway conditions in the United States since 1932, was required to pay income tax before sailing for Europe. Yamamoto posted a bond on September 18 to secure his departure after protesting the departure from past exemption practices. The Embassy requests the Secretary's good offices in resolving the tax issue and releasing the obligation.
subfiles.title: Note No. 185 from Japanese Embassy regarding Departure Bond of Yorio Yamamoto

subfiles.about: Transmits the Japanese Chargé d'Affaires' note to the Treasury Department and requests consideration for releasing Yamamoto's departure bond.
subfiles.summary: Under Secretary of State William Phillips transmits to Secretary of the Treasury Henry Morgenthau, Jr. a copy of the Japanese Embassy's note of September 25, 1934. Phillips requests that Treasury consider the matter and arrange to release the bond deposited by Yorio Yamamoto if he can be exempted in accordance with departmental practice in similar cases.
subfiles.title: Letter from Under Secretary of State to Secretary of the Treasury regarding Yamamoto's Bond

subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Japanese Embassy's note regarding Yorio Yamamoto and states the matter has been referred to appropriate authorities.
subfiles.summary: Under Secretary William Phillips acknowledges receipt of Japanese Embassy note No. 185 concerning the requirement that Yorio Yamamoto deposit a bond for income taxes prior to sailing for Europe. Phillips informs the Japanese Chargé d'Affaires that the matter has been referred to the appropriate government authorities and that further communication will follow.
subfiles.title: Note from Under Secretary of State to Japanese Chargé d'Affaires ad interim

subfiles.about: States that the general taxability of non-diplomatic foreign representatives is under review and a decision on Yamamoto will follow.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of the Treasury Stephen B. Gibbons acknowledges Under Secretary Phillips' letter of October 3, 1934. He states that the question of taxing compensation received by non-diplomatic foreign representatives in the United States is receiving careful consideration by the Treasury Department. The State Department will be advised regarding Yamamoto's liability and the release of his bond once a conclusion is reached.
subfiles.title: Letter from Treasury Department regarding Tax Liability of Non-Diplomatic Representatives

subfiles.about: Informs the Japanese Ambassador that the Treasury Department is currently considering the taxability of compensation received by non-diplomatic foreign representatives.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of State William Phillips refers to the Japanese Embassy's note of September 25, 1934 regarding Yorio Yamamoto. He informs Ambassador Saito that appropriate United States authorities are carefully considering the general taxability of non-diplomatic foreign representatives. Phillips promises to communicate further as soon as a final decision is reached regarding Yamamoto's case.
subfiles.title: Note from Acting Secretary of State to Japanese Ambassador regarding Tax Review

subfiles.about: Inquires whether Treasury can continue exempting Japanese officials pending a decision and whether a reciprocal agreement should be pursued.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary Phillips reports that Takaharu Ito of the Japanese Embassy called to propose negotiations for a reciprocal agreement exempting non-diplomatic officials from income taxation. Phillips notes that both governments have historically exempted each other's officials on official income. He asks Secretary Morgenthau whether Japanese officials can continue to receive exemptions pending a decision and whether a reciprocal agreement should be concluded if exemption is unavailable under current law.
subfiles.title: Letter from Acting Secretary of State to Secretary of the Treasury on Reciprocal Exemption

subfiles.about: Records a conversation with Takaharu Ito regarding Japan's desire to negotiate a reciprocal tax exemption agreement for unaccredited officials.
subfiles.summary: Takaharu Ito of the Japanese Embassy met with State Department officers to propose negotiating a reciprocal agreement exempting officials without diplomatic or consular status from income taxation. He highlighted recent difficulties experienced by Japanese officials required to post bonds before departing due to retroactive tax levies. Ito also inquired about the number of American non-diplomatic officials in Japan, and the State Department agreed to investigate.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on Proposed Reciprocal Tax Exemption Agreement

subfiles.about: Reports that inquiries among principal U.S. departments revealed only two Treasury employees in Japan with status comparable to the Japanese officials.
subfiles.summary: Inquiries to principal government departments revealed only two Treasury employees in Japan whose status appeared comparable to that of the Japanese officials in question. Mr. Sturgeon had anticipated a formal note from the Japanese Embassy, but none was received. Mr. Ito was informed of these findings by telephone.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Inquiries regarding American Personnel in Japan

subfiles.about: Handwritten note regarding internal departmental coordination on tax matters.
subfiles.summary: A brief internal handwritten note within the Division of Far Eastern Affairs concerning coordination between departmental officers regarding the tax status of foreign officials.
subfiles.title: Internal Note regarding Tax Exemption Discussions

subfiles.about: Requests a list of persons in Japan holding special passports who do not possess diplomatic or consular status.
subfiles.summary: William R. Vallance of the Legal Adviser's Office requests that Mr. Scanlan of the Passport Division provide a list of persons holding special passports in Japan who do not enjoy diplomatic or consular status.
subfiles.title: Inquiry to Passport Division regarding Special Passports Held in Japan

subfiles.about: Explains why an accurate list of special passport holders in Japan cannot be provided from passport files and suggests other sources.
subfiles.summary: The Passport Division reports that it cannot provide an accurate list of non-diplomatic special passport holders in Japan because individuals frequently fail to surrender passports upon terminating their duties. Such individuals likely include naval and marine officers not serving as attaches, trade commissioners, and embassy or consular clerks. The division suggests consulting the Navy Department, Commerce Department, and Foreign Service Administration directly.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Passport Division on Special Passports in Japan

subfiles.about: States that Yorio Yamamoto is taxable under ruling I.T. 2018 regarding commercial enterprises and defers opinion on reciprocal agreements.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of the Treasury Josephine Roche informs Secretary Hull that records indicate Yorio Yamamoto was manager of the Japanese Government Railways office in New York, a commercial enterprise. Under Treasury ruling I.T. 2018, employees of foreign government commercial enterprises are nonresident aliens liable for Federal income tax. Regarding reciprocal exemptions and future agreements, Treasury defers a definite reply pending the outcome of interdepartmental conferences between State and Treasury representatives.
subfiles.title: Letter from Treasury Department regarding Tax Liability of Yorio Yamamoto

subfiles.about: Requests that four Japanese railway officials in New York be permitted to post bonds in lieu of paying income taxes pending a final policy decision.
subfiles.summary: Japanese Ambassador Hirosi Saito requests the Secretary of State's good offices regarding four officials of the Japanese Department of Railways stationed in New York: K. Dan, S. Nagata, H. Nishioka, and S. Fujii. The Ambassador asks that these officials be permitted to file bonds in lieu of paying income taxes until the taxability of non-diplomatic foreign representatives is officially determined.
subfiles.title: Note No. 225 from Japanese Ambassador regarding Departure Bonds for Four Officials

subfiles.about: Instructs diplomatic officers to report foreign laws on the taxation of consular and non-diplomatic officials to support proposed congressional legislation.
subfiles.summary: Diplomatic Serial No. 2497 reviews the Treasury Department's decision abandoning non-statutory reciprocal tax exemptions for consular and non-diplomatic personnel under Article 641 of Regulations 77. To prepare legislation for the upcoming session of Congress, American diplomatic officers are urgently instructed to compile and report all local statutes, decrees, and regulations concerning the taxation of official compensation of American personnel abroad. Officers must also report the number and salaries of non-diplomatic personnel stationed in the United States by their host governments who would be affected by the Treasury ruling.
subfiles.title: Diplomatic Serial No. 2497: Taxation of Official Compensation of Foreign Personnel

subfiles.about: Transmits Ambassador Saito's note requesting permission for four Japanese railway officials to file bonds in lieu of income tax payments.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of State William Phillips refers to Treasury's letter of November 26 and the postponement of decisions on unaccredited foreign officials. Phillips transmits a copy of Ambassador Saito's note of December 3, 1934 concerning Japanese railway officials K. Dan, S. Nagata, H. Nishioka, and S. Fujii. He asks whether Treasury will permit these officials to deposit bonds in lieu of paying income taxes pending a final determination of the taxability question.
subfiles.title: Letter from Acting Secretary of State to Secretary of the Treasury regarding Four Officials

subfiles.about: Acknowledges Ambassador Saito's note requesting that four railway officials be permitted to file bonds and states the request was referred to Treasury.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull acknowledges receipt of Ambassador Saito's note No. 225 of December 3, 1934. Hull informs the Ambassador that the request to permit four Japanese railway officials stationed in New York to file bonds in lieu of paying income taxes has been submitted to the appropriate government authorities, and promises further communication upon receipt of a reply.
subfiles.title: Note from Secretary of State to Japanese Ambassador Acknowledging Bond Request

subfiles.about: Transmits to Ambassador Grew copies of correspondence exchanged with the Japanese Embassy and Treasury regarding tax exemptions for non-diplomatic personnel.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary Phillips refers to Diplomatic Serial No. 2497 of November 15, 1934 and transmits to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo copies of recent correspondence with the Japanese Embassy and the Treasury Department. Phillips explains that the background correspondence relates to the taxability of Japanese unaccredited officials and notes that further instructions will be sent if negotiating a reciprocal agreement proves advisable.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 651 to American Ambassador in Tokyo regarding Tax Exemption

subfiles.about: Informs the State Department that the Collector of Internal Revenue in New York has accepted surety bonds for the four Japanese railway officials.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of the Treasury Josephine Roche replies to Under Secretary Phillips' inquiry of December 13, 1934. She informs the State Department that records show the Collector of Internal Revenue at the Customhouse in New York accepted surety bonds dated October 5, 1934 for Japanese railway officials K. Dan, S. Nagata, H. Nishioka, and S. Fujii to guarantee payment of any taxes due.
subfiles.title: Letter from Treasury Department regarding Acceptance of Bonds for Four Officials

subfiles.about: Informs the Japanese Ambassador that surety bonds have been accepted in New York for the four Department of Railways officials.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull refers to Ambassador Saito's note of December 3, 1934 concerning railway officials K. Dan, S. Nagata, H. Nishioka, and S. Fujii. Hull informs the Ambassador that the Collector of Internal Revenue at the Customhouse in New York accepted surety bonds dated October 5, 1934 for each official as guarantee for payment of any taxes due, pending a final decision on their liability.
subfiles.title: Note from Secretary of State to Japanese Ambassador on Accepted Bonds

subfiles.about: Details a Japanese proposal to effect reciprocal tax exemption through an exchange of notes based on executive authority without statutory amendment.
subfiles.summary: Takaharu Ito informed Eugene H. Dooman that the Japanese Foreign Office and Department of Finance agreed that while Japanese tax law mandates taxing unaccredited foreign officials, exemption could be granted through an exchange of diplomatic notes reciprocally waiving taxes. Dooman responded that U.S. Treasury authorities believe statutory amendments to the Revenue Act are required before exemptions can be granted. Ito indicated he would provide an informal draft note and requested that the proposal be kept confidential.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on Proposed Reciprocal Tax Exemption through Notes

subfiles.about: Recommends informing the Japanese Embassy that their proposal is being considered while awaiting potential legislative action in Congress.
subfiles.summary: Eugene H. Dooman transmits to William R. Vallance of the Legal Adviser's Office his memorandum of conversation with Takaharu Ito and the attached Japanese draft note. Noting Treasury's view that current revenue laws preclude an executive agreement, Dooman recommends informing the Embassy that the matter is under consideration and sharing a copy of the bill once submitted to Congress. He asks whether Vallance concurs in this proposed response.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Dooman to Vallance regarding Japanese Tax Exemption Proposal

subfiles.about: Records informing Takaharu Ito that existing revenue laws prevent an executive tax exemption agreement and that legislative amendments are being explored.
subfiles.summary: Eugene H. Dooman met with Takaharu Ito to convey the Department's appreciation for the Japanese Embassy's suggested exchange of notes. Dooman explained that the Treasury Department maintains that the Revenue Act does not permit granting tax exemptions to unaccredited Japanese officials, but noted that the State Department is exploring ways to bring about an arrangement, including possible statutory amendments. Ito thanked him and requested further information as soon as available.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Takaharu Ito regarding Tax Exemption Procedure

subfiles.about: Inquires whether Assistant Secretary Carr has signed the letter proposing an amendment to the Revenue Act to exempt non-diplomatic officials.
subfiles.summary: William R. Vallance writes a brief note inquiring whether Assistant Secretary Wilbur J. Carr has signed the letter concerning the proposed amendment to the Revenue Act to exempt non-diplomatic foreign officials from income tax.
subfiles.title: Inquiry regarding Letter on Revenue Act Amendment

subfiles.about: Confirms that Assistant Secretary Carr signed the letter to Donald Richberg regarding the draft Revenue Act amendment.
subfiles.summary: Miss deLashmutt informs William R. Vallance that Assistant Secretary Wilbur J. Carr signed the Department's letter to Executive Assistant Donald Richberg concerning the draft bill amending the Revenue Act.
subfiles.title: Note confirming Signature of Letter to Donald Richberg

subfiles.about: Inquires whether Japanese Embassy tax correspondence can be filed pending the introduction of the revenue amendment bill in Congress.
subfiles.summary: William R. Vallance informs Eugene H. Dooman that Assistant Secretary Carr signed the letter to Donald Richberg requesting approval of the draft revenue amendment bill. Vallance asks whether Takaharu Ito's letter of January 19, 1935 and related memoranda can now be filed pending the bill's introduction in Congress. An internal endorsement indicates approval to hold or file the documents.
subfiles.title: Memorandum regarding Filing of Tax Exemption Papers Pending Legislation

subfiles.about: Transmits an informal draft note proposing reciprocal tax exemption through administrative executive action rather than a formal treaty.
subfiles.summary: Takaharu Ito writes informally to Eugene H. Dooman transmitting a draft note on mutual tax exemption for government officials. Ito explains that to avoid the complexities of a formal treaty, the Japanese Government desires to effect the understanding by each country internally invoking its executive powers to grant exemption and notifying the other. He emphasizes that Japan considers it undesirable to make the understanding public and requests that Dooman negotiate with Treasury authorities accordingly.
subfiles.title: Informal Letter from Takaharu Ito Transmitting Draft Note on Tax Exemption

subfiles.about: Proposes that Japan and the United States reciprocally exempt officials from income taxes on official compensation, excluding private business income.
subfiles.summary: A draft diplomatic note stating that the Japanese Department of Finance is prepared to exempt United States officials in Japan from taxes on income received for official services, provided reciprocal treatment is accorded to Japanese officials in the United States. The proposal explicitly excludes from exemption any income derived from profitable private business pursuits.
subfiles.title: Draft Note from Japanese Embassy on Reciprocal Tax Exemption

subfiles.about: Records Japanese Third Secretary Kawahara presenting 1918 Treasury rulings exempting Japanese officials and discussing pending congressional legislation.
subfiles.summary: Shun-ichiro Kawahara presented 1918 correspondence showing that the Bureau of Internal Revenue previously ruled Japanese military and official personnel exempt from income tax, inquiring whether this precedent could be raised with Treasury. Dooman advised against reviving an executive arrangement and explained that legislation was being introduced in Congress to provide reciprocal tax exemptions. Dooman warned that seeking an executive agreement would cause unnecessary difficulties, and Kawahara agreed to await the congressional bill.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on 1918 Precedent for Tax Exemption

subfiles.about: Inquires whether Japanese military, naval, and official personnel residing in the United States on official missions are exempt from income tax.
subfiles.summary: Minoru Fujii of the Japanese Embassy writes informally to Commissioner of Internal Revenue Daniel C. Roper. He inquires whether Japanese naval and military officers and other officials sent on official missions and residing in the United States should be exempt from Federal income tax since their incomes derive from Japanese Imperial Government sources.
subfiles.title: Letter from Minoru Fujii to Commissioner Roper on Tax Exemption

subfiles.about: Rules that Japanese officials on temporary official missions receiving no income from U.S. sources are not subject to Federal income tax.
subfiles.summary: Commissioner of Internal Revenue Daniel C. Roper informs Minoru Fujii that Japanese naval and military officers and other officials performing special official missions in the United States will not be subject to Federal income tax. The ruling applies to temporary personnel ordered by the Japanese Government who are not permanently situated in the country and receive no income from United States sources.
subfiles.title: Letter from Commissioner Roper Ruling Japanese Officials Exempt from Tax

subfiles.about: Expresses the Japanese Embassy's gratitude for Commissioner Roper's ruling exempting Japanese officials on special missions from income tax.
subfiles.summary: Minoru Fujii acknowledges Commissioner Roper's letter of March 26, 1918 confirming that Japanese military, naval, and civil officials on special government missions are not subject to the income tax law. Fujii expresses the gratitude of the Japanese Embassy for the courtesy extended.
subfiles.title: Letter from Minoru Fujii Acknowledging Tax Exemption Ruling

subfiles.about: Asks Eugene H. Dooman's opinion on pending tax exemption legislation.
subfiles.summary: William R. Vallance sends a brief handwritten routing note to Eugene H. Dooman inquiring about his opinion on the pending tax exemption legislation. Dooman writes a note concurring that the proposed arrangement is satisfactory.
subfiles.title: Routing Note from Vallance to Dooman on Pending Legislation

subfiles.about: Proposes amending Section 116 of the Revenue Act of 1934 to grant reciprocal income tax exemption to foreign government employees.
subfiles.summary: Representative Robert L. Doughton introduces H.R. 7998 in the House of Representatives, amending section 116 of the Revenue Act of 1934 to exclude from gross income the compensation of foreign government employees, including consular and non-diplomatic representatives. Exemption is conditioned on non-citizenship, performance of services similar to those of American officials abroad, and the foreign government granting equivalent exemptions to U.S. personnel. The bill directs the Secretary of State to certify qualifying countries and services to Treasury, and applies retroactively under prior revenue acts.
subfiles.title: House Bill H.R. 7998: Exemption of Compensation of Foreign Employees
subfiles.to: Committee on Ways and Means, House of Representatives

subfiles.about: Inquires whether Japanese Department of Railways officials and technical experts would qualify for tax exemption under pending bill H.R. 7998.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Hirosi Saito asks whether Section 1(2) of H.R. 7998 would cover Japanese Department of Railways officials whose duties involve studying railway communication and transportation systems. He also inquires whether a technical expert in New York inspecting purchased goods would qualify. The Ambassador maintains that these duties should be included under the terms of the bill even though the United States Government maintains no Department of Railways.
subfiles.title: Note No. 108 from Japanese Ambassador Inquiry regarding Scope of H.R. 7998

subfiles.about: Urges early committee action on H.R. 7998, citing threatened foreign taxation of American Treasury personnel in Vienna.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary Phillips writes to Chairman Robert L. Doughton urging early committee consideration of H.R. 7998. He cites a dispatch from Vienna reporting that an American Treasury representative there is threatened with local taxation while the legislation remains pending. Quoting Secretary Hull, Phillips explains that ending reciprocal exemptions would subject American personnel abroad to heavy foreign taxes, and emphasizes that the bill merely continues a decade-long administrative practice.
subfiles.title: Letter from Acting Secretary of State to Representative Doughton on H.R. 7998

subfiles.about: Transmits the Japanese Ambassador's inquiry and recommends interpreting H.R. 7998 liberally to exempt Japanese railway officials.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull transmits to Chairman Doughton a copy of Ambassador Saito's note of June 19, 1935 regarding Japanese railway officials under H.R. 7998. Hull states that U.S. consular officers perform somewhat similar reporting functions in Japan and indicates his readiness to give the bill a liberal interpretation by certifying that Japan grants equivalent exemptions. He urges Doughton to consider clarifying the bill if necessary, arguing that the meager revenue obtained would be far outweighed by diplomatic friction.
subfiles.title: Letter from Secretary of State to Representative Doughton regarding Railway Officials

subfiles.about: Acknowledges Ambassador Saito's inquiry regarding H.R. 7998 and promises further communication after consideration.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull acknowledges receipt of Ambassador Saito's note No. 108 of June 19, 1935 inquiring whether Japanese Department of Railways officials fall within the exemption terms of H.R. 7998. Hull states that the matter is receiving attention and that the Department will communicate with the Ambassador again at a later date.
subfiles.title: Note from Secretary of State to Japanese Ambassador Acknowledging Inquiry on H.R. 7998

subfiles.about: Expresses the opinion that H.R. 7998 is sufficient to cover Japanese railway officials if consular reporting is certified as similar.
subfiles.summary: Chairman Robert L. Doughton replies to Secretary Hull's letter of July 5, stating his opinion that H.R. 7998 in its present form is sufficient to exempt Japanese railway officials, provided the Secretary of State certifies that U.S. consular offices in Japan perform similar services. Doughton encloses an advisory report from Lovell H. Parker, Chief of Staff of the Joint Committee on Internal Revenue Taxation, and suggests taking up the matter directly with Treasury.
subfiles.title: Letter from Representative Doughton to Secretary of State on Railway Officials

subfiles.about: Reports on Treasury concerns regarding commercial representatives and advises against redrafting H.R. 7998 to avoid widening exemptions.
subfiles.summary: Lovell H. Parker reports to Chairman Doughton regarding Secretary Hull's letter on Japanese railway officials. Parker explains that during drafting, the Treasury Department insisted on limiting exemptions to prevent foreign commercial agents, such as Soviet commercial representatives, from claiming tax immunity. Parker advises that certification by the Secretary of State that U.S. consular officers perform similar reporting duties will suffice to cover Japanese railway officials, and warns strongly against redrafting the bill in a way that might inadvertently exempt commercial entities.
subfiles.title: Report from Lovell H. Parker to Chairman Doughton on Scope of H.R. 7998

subfiles.about: Informs Chairman Doughton that the State Department has consulted Treasury regarding his interpretation of H.R. 7998.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of State William Phillips replies to Chairman Doughton's letter of July 11 regarding H.R. 7998 and Japanese railway officials. Phillips states that the Department has addressed a communication to the Secretary of the Treasury to ascertain his position on Doughton's interpretation, promising to communicate further upon receiving Treasury's reply.
subfiles.title: Letter from Acting Secretary of State to Representative Doughton on Treasury Position

subfiles.about: Asks whether Treasury concurs with Chairman Doughton that H.R. 7998 covers Japanese railway officials under State Department certification.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of State William Phillips transmits to Secretary Morgenthau copies of recent correspondence with Japanese Ambassador Saito and Ways and Means Chairman Doughton regarding H.R. 7998. Phillips asks whether the Treasury Department concurs in Chairman Doughton's view that the bill is sufficient in its present form to exempt Japanese railway officials, provided the Secretary of State certifies that American consular officers in Japan perform similar services.
subfiles.title: Letter from Acting Secretary of State to Secretary of the Treasury on H.R. 7998

subfiles.about: Compares Senate Bill S. 2762 and House Bill H.R. 7998, recommending support for the House bill due to retroactive exemption and constitutional origin.
subfiles.summary: A Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum reports that S. 2762 passed the Senate on June 24, 1935, while H.R. 7998 is pending before the House Ways and Means Committee. The memorandum notes that H.R. 7998 includes a retroactive exemption feature strongly favored by Legal Adviser Vallance. In addition, because the bill affects revenue and properly originates in the House, the State Department considers passage of the House bill distinctly preferable.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Senate and House Bills for Tax Exemption of Foreign Employees

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Under Secretary Phillips' conversation with Ambassador Saito regarding pending tax legislation.
subfiles.summary: A Department of State Document File Note cross-referencing file 811.512394 Shipping/49. The note records that Japanese Ambassador Saito, in conversation with Under Secretary Phillips on July 1, 1935, expressed his government's interest in the tax exemption bill pending in Congress and hoped for its enactment.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Cross-Reference to Phillips-Saito Conversation of July 1, 1935

subfiles.about: Transmits excerpt of conversation with Japanese Ambassador and reports uncertain legislative prospects for the tax exemption bill.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State refers to Diplomatic Serial No. 2497 and transmits to the American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim in Tokyo an excerpt of Under Secretary Phillips' conversation of July 1, 1935 with Japanese Ambassador Saito. The instruction notes that due to heavy legislative pressure in Congress, the prospects for the bill's passage during the current session remain uncertain.
subfiles.title: Instruction to American Chargé d'Affaires in Tokyo on Tax Legislation
subfiles.to: American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Records the Japanese Ambassador's expression of interest in pending tax legislation for Japanese railway and Treasury officials.
subfiles.summary: Under Secretary of State William Phillips records that Japanese Ambassador Saito expressed his government's keen interest in the pending congressional bill providing reciprocal tax relief for Japanese officials in the United States and American officials in Japan. The Ambassador specifically mentioned Japanese Treasury experts and railway employees, expressing hope that action could be taken to assure passage of the legislation.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Under Secretary Phillips and Ambassador Saito

subfiles.about: Acknowledges State Department inquiry on H.R. 7998 and reports the matter is under active consideration.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of the Treasury T. Jefferson Coolidge acknowledges the State Department's letter regarding H.R. 7998 and Chairman Doughton's interpretation concerning Japanese railway officials. He states that the question of whether Treasury concurs in Doughton's view is under active consideration, and promises to apprise the State Department as soon as a conclusion is reached.
subfiles.title: Letter from Treasury Department regarding Consideration of H.R. 7998 Interpretation

subfiles.about: Confirms enactment of H.R. 7998 on August 27, 1935 and agrees that Japanese railway officials qualify upon State Department certification.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of the Treasury T. Jefferson Coolidge reports that H.R. 7998 was passed by Congress and signed into law by the President on August 27, 1935. Treasury concurs in Chairman Doughton's view that the new statute is sufficient to exempt Japanese Department of Railways officials, provided the Secretary of State certifies that American consular officers in Japan perform similar services and other statutory requirements (non-citizenship and reciprocal exemption) are met. Coolidge notes the certification procedures required by the new law.
subfiles.title: Letter from Treasury Department Concurring in Exemption of Railway Officials

subfiles.about: Transmits draft reply note to Japanese Ambassador incorporating terms of the newly enacted reciprocal tax exemption law.
subfiles.summary: William R. Vallance transmits a draft note to be sent to the Japanese Ambassador in response to the Embassy's provisional draft note, tracking the language of the Act approved August 27, 1935. Vallance notes Treasury's confirmation of September 5 that Japanese railway officials will be exempt once the Secretary of State certifies similar consular functions. He suggests securing Treasury's approval of the draft note prior to transmission and notes Treasury may require the Embassy to supply names and duties of arriving officials claiming exemption.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Legal Adviser on Draft Note to Japan under Act of August 27, 1935

subfiles.about: Submits draft tax exemption note to the Legal Adviser for review.
subfiles.summary: William R. Vallance submits the draft note and associated papers concerning the reciprocal tax exemption agreement with Japan to Legal Adviser Green H. Hackworth for review and approval.
subfiles.title: Routing Slip from Vallance to Hackworth regarding Draft Note

subfiles.about: Proposes formal notification that the Secretary of State has certified Japan for reciprocal income tax exemptions under the Act of August 27, 1935.
subfiles.summary: A draft diplomatic note acknowledging the Japanese Ambassador's communication stating Japan's readiness to exempt American government employees from income taxes on official salaries. In response, the Secretary of State confirms that under the Act of Congress approved August 27, 1935, he has certified to the Secretary of the Treasury that Japan grants equivalent exemptions and described the character of American official services in Japan, thereby establishing reciprocal tax exemption for qualifying Japanese officials in the United States.
subfiles.title: Draft Note from Secretary of State to Japanese Ambassador on Reciprocal Exemption

subfiles.about: Explains attached Japanese draft note and Embassy request for a provisional draft of the State Department's proposed reply.
subfiles.summary: A departmental note attaching a draft note that the Japanese Embassy proposes to submit once approved by the Japanese Foreign Office and Department of Finance. The note explains that the Embassy requested to see a provisional draft of the reply the State Department would make before formally submitting their note.
subfiles.title: Cover Note on Proposed Exchange of Notes with Japanese Embassy
